questions.questionText: What is the key advantage hierarchical clustering has over k-means?
options: You don't need to choose the number of clusters before running it — you can cut the resulting dendrogram at any level afterward
It never requires a distance metric
questions.correctAnswer: You don't need to choose the number of clusters before running it — you can cut the resulting dendrogram at any level afterward
questions.explanation: Agglomerative clustering builds the entire merge tree first; the number of clusters is decided by where you cut that tree, after the fact.

questions.questionText: What does the "linkage" method control in agglomerative clustering?
options: How the distance between two clusters (not individual points) is defined when deciding what to merge next
questions.correctAnswer: How the distance between two clusters (not individual points) is defined when deciding what to merge next
questions.explanation: Since clusters (not just points) need to be compared once merging starts, linkage (single, complete, average, Ward's) defines what "distance between two clusters" even means.

questions.questionText: What's the main practical drawback of hierarchical clustering compared to k-means?
options: It can't be used for numeric data
It's typically much more computationally expensive (roughly O(n^3)), making it impractical on very large datasets
It cannot produce more than 2 clusters
questions.correctAnswer: It's typically much more computationally expensive (roughly O(n^3)), making it impractical on very large datasets
questions.explanation: Naive agglomerative clustering scales cubically with the number of points, far worse than k-means' near-linear per-iteration cost.
